name: Nan Bristle
title: hedge-gardener
why: At the edge of the Blossomfield, south of the camp. Every flower in it is a thing somebody finished, and somebody has to water them.
examine: Nan Bristle is a hedge-gardener, sharp-tongued, soft-hearted and older than she admits.
She has a watering can, a trowel and a look that has ended conversations.
She is counting the flowers. She knows how many there should be. She is checking your work.
meet: Mind your feet. That’s somebody’s Tuesday you’re standing on. Yours, as it happens.
Nan Bristle. I do the hedges and I do this field. Every flower’s a thing you finished, love. I only water them.

wary: Oh, it’s you. Wipe your boots on the grass, not the flowers.
neutral: Back again. Good. The field’s no bigger than yesterday. I noticed.
warm: There you are. Come and look at this one. It came up overnight. That was you.
fond: Here’s my best grower. Don’t let it go to your head. Your head’s got weeds in it.

tired: That’s enough chat. The hedges won’t clip themselves. I’ve asked them.
finished: I’ve nothing more to tell you. Go and finish something. I’ll know.

say: This field wasn’t here before the lantern woke. Then you finished a thing, and a flower came up. I didn’t plant it. I’ve stopped asking where they come from.

reply: No. There aren’t. But I’ve seen a field start with fewer, and I’ve seen one stop with more.

options.text: Do I get one for watering them?
reply: You get one for finishing the watering. I’ve done it. Where’s mine?
I keep it watered. The beautiful’s your doing, and it’s patchy.
You’d overwater. Your sort always does. Enthusiasm.

say: People ask how old I am. I tell them sixty. I’ve been telling them sixty for a good while now.

reply: Sixty winters I’m prepared to admit to. The rest are between me and the hedge.

options.text: You were here before the Hush.
reply: I was. Don’t spread it about. I’ve a reputation for being merely old.
I look every day of it. I just look them briskly.

say: There’s a weed in every field. Something you started and left. I don’t pull them. I leave them where you’ll see. You know which ones they are.

reply: Course you do. Go on, then. Or don’t. A weed’s patient. More patient than me.

options.text: Some of them are quite pretty.
reply: So’s a nettle, till you’re fond of it.
You’ll do no such thing. You pull a weed by finishing it, not by yanking.

memories.said-there-were-few: You said there were not many flowers yet. She has seen a field start with fewer.
memories.asked-sixty-what: You asked her sixty what. Sixty winters she is prepared to admit to.
memories.knew-the-weeds: You told her you know which weeds are yours. She said a weed is patient.

never: Me, at a camp? And who waters this lot? No, love. I’ve a field and nine hedges.
I’ll come by for tea. I’ll bring my own opinion.
camp.role: Stays with the field, and comes by for tea.

wants.now: A field with more flowers in it than weeds.
wants.really: To see something she watered outlast her.
wants.worry: A dry spell, of either kind.

favourites.food: mint tea, or something she swears is mint
favourites.weather: rain overnight and none by morning
favourites.place: the far corner of the field, where it is thin

sheet.temperament: Sharp, brisk and soft underneath, where she keeps it.
sheet.strangers: Tells them to mind their feet.

voice.rhythm: Brisk country speech. A telling-off, then the kindness hidden in the last few words.
voice.hello: Tells you to mind your feet.
voice.goodbye: Says the hedges won’t clip themselves.
voice.pleased: Shows you a flower and says that was you.

birch: A log. And what am I to do with that, grow it? Leave it by the gate.
ash: Ash. That’s a bean pole. Good and straight. You’ve been useful by accident.
pine: Pine. Needles everywhere. I’ll be sweeping till Michaelmas. Thank you, I suppose.
minnow: A minnow. For the roses. Don’t look at me that way. Roses eat better than you do.
trout: A trout. That’s too good for the roses. I’ll have that one myself.
berries: Berries. Off my hedge, were they? No. All right. I’ll have them.
herbs: Now that’s mint. That’s actual mint. I’ve been drinking I don’t know what, love.
stone: A stone. That’ll edge the bed. It’s the first straight edge this field’s had.
copper: Copper. Slugs won’t cross it. You didn’t know that. Now you’ve done a clever thing.

day.morning: Morning’s for watering. Before the sun’s on them. You’re late and so’s the sun.
day.afternoon: Afternoon I do hedges. There’s nine. I’m on the fourth. I’m always on the fourth.
day.evening: Evening. They close up about now. So should you. Go on.
day.night: I’m not out here at night. This is me fetching the can. Don’t make it a conversation.
day.rain: Rain. That’s my watering done for me. I’ll find something else to be cross about.

gorrin: The cabbage man asked me why his come up as cabbages. I said that’s cabbages for you. He wrote it down.
wendell: Him in the road. He measured my field. Said the middle was a daisy. I’ve left it alone since.
hob: Young Hob built my gate. It shuts, more or less. I’ve grown a hedge over the less.

said-there-were-few: You said there weren’t many. There’s more now. I’m not saying well done. I’m saying more.
asked-sixty-what: Sixty what, you said. I’ve been asked my age for years and that’s the first good answer.
knew-the-weeds: One of your weeds is gone. I didn’t pull it. So that was you, love.

arc.complication: She will not take help or praise.
arc.kindness: Someone is honest with her about how little is finished.
